title: Leonardo's Spatial Grammar: A CAD Reverse-Engineering Analysis Corpus: Leonardo's CAD, Leonardo's Rulers, Leonardo's Score
text:
Leonardo's Spatial Grammar: A CAD Reverse-Engineering Analysis Corpus: Leonardo's CAD, Leonardo's Rulers, Leonardo's Score.   Abstract (it)  Il corpus in esame decostruisce il mito dell'applicazione standardizzata della prospettiva albertiana a base quadrata nell'opera di Leonardo da Vinci, proponendo un paradigma metrico-modulare fondato su evidenze geometriche oggettive e falsificabili. Attraverso l'analisi tridimensionale dell'Annunciazione, dell'Adorazione dei Magi e dell'Ultima Cena, emerge una grammatica spaziale in costante evoluzione. Leonardo abbandona la rigida scacchiera per sviluppare un sistema di "righelli inseriti", evolvendo da una misurazione monodirezionale a un'architettura ritmica e stereometrica. Il metodo d'indagine, basato su tecniche di retro-ingegneria CAD e sul "banale aristotelico", dimostra come le proporzioni spaziali (dal modulo 4:3 ai ritmi polifonici 1:4:1 e 2:1:2) siano direttamente ricavabili dall'opera stessa. L'approccio restituisce spazi non solo misurabili, ma architettonicamente rimontabili e strutturati sulle misure umane, rigettando interpretazioni esoteriche o simbologie forzate. 
  Abstract (en)  The examined corpus deconstructs the myth of the standardized application of Albertian square-based perspective in the works of Leonardo da Vinci, proposing a metric-modular paradigm founded on objective and falsifiable geometric evidence. Through the three-dimensional analysis of the Annunciation, the Adoration of the Magi, and the Last Supper, a constantly evolving spatial grammar emerges. Leonardo abandons the rigid checkerboard to develop a system of "inserted rulers," evolving from a monodirectional measurement to a rhythmic and stereometric architecture. The investigative method, based on CAD reverse-engineering techniques and the "Aristotelian obvious," demonstrates how spatial proportions (from the 4:3 module to the 1:4:1 and 2:1:2 polyphonic rhythms) can be directly derived from the artwork itself. This approach yields spaces that are not only measurable but architecturally reassemblable and structured on human measurements, rejecting esoteric interpretations or forced symbolism. 
   
 Abstract esteso (IT) 
 Il corpus  Leonardo's CAD, Leonardo's Rulers, Leonardo's Score  propone una rilettura unitaria di tre indagini nate separatamente ma convergenti verso una stessa ipotesi: Leonardo da Vinci non applica in modo meccanico la prospettiva albertiana a maglia quadrata, né se ne discosta episodicamente per errore o licenza, ma sviluppa progressivamente una propria grammatica spaziale metrico-modulare, verificabile a partire dall'immagine stessa. L'oggetto della ricerca non è una lettura iconografica complessiva delle opere, bensì la ricostruzione degli spazi dipinti come dispositivi misurabili, abitabili e rimontabili attraverso procedure geometriche esplicite. 
 Il trittico mette in relazione tre momenti distinti di questa elaborazione: l’ Annunciazione  come forma prototipica della “geometria inserita”, l’ Adorazione dei Magi  come emersione di una griglia generativa 4:3 connessa al braccio fiorentino, e l’ Ultima Cena  come approdo a una vera polifonia stereometrica, governata da un unico modulo capace di coordinare larghezza, altezza e profondità. In questa prospettiva, lo sviluppo dell’opera leonardesca appare come una sequenza coerente: da uno spazio ancora concentrato e leggibile attraverso pochi regoli incorporati, a un’architettura figurata sempre più complessa, immersiva e ritmica. 
 Sul piano metodologico, il corpus assume come principio guida il “banale aristotelico”: partire esclusivamente da ciò che nel dipinto è visibile, misurabile e geometricamente controllabile, senza ricorrere a simbologie arbitrarie, geometrie occulte o sovrastrutture interpretative non falsificabili. Il metodo combina osservazione diretta delle tracce figurative, geometria inversa, retro-ingegneria CAD e verifiche di coerenza antropometrica, zoometrica e architettonica; il punto decisivo è che gli elementi pittorici — bugne, mattonelle, cassettoni, arazzi, arcate, scale — vengono assunti non come semplici dettagli scenografici, ma come strumenti metrici lasciati visibili all’interno dell’opera. 
 Nell’ Annunciazione  questa logica si manifesta nella nicchia che accoglie Maria. Le bugne e le piastrelle costruiscono un sistema di riferimento ortogonale e consentono di definire il modulo q, pari a mezzo braccio fiorentino, da cui derivano la profondità visibile, l’apertura, la larghezza complessiva e la quota dell’orizzonte. La nicchia non è dunque una quinta secondaria, ma una scatola spaziale rettangolare calibrata sul corpo della Vergine: la figura non occupa semplicemente lo spazio, ma ne condivide la misura, al punto che l’orizzonte coincide con la sua spalla seduta e le stesse anomalie anatomiche tradizionalmente segnalate si ridimensionano entro un sistema antropometrico coerente. 
 Nell’ Adorazione dei Magi , invece, il nodo interpretativo riguarda il superamento della griglia quadrata tradizionalmente assunta come base prospettica del foglio Uffizi 436 E. L’analisi proposta sostiene che una maglia rettangolare in rapporto 4:3, ancorata al braccio fiorentino, restituisca coerenza alle arcate, elimini deformazioni interpretate come errori e consenta di comprendere l’innesto di triangoli aurei e geometrie pentagonali nella costruzione delle scale. Lo spazio risulta così non solo figurativamente suggestivo, ma architettonicamente progettato: un impianto nel quale proporzione pratica e tensione armonica convivono senza contraddizione. 
 Nel  Cenacolo  il sistema evolve ulteriormente. Il corpus sostiene che la lettura fondata sulla maglia quadrata, adottata anche in studi precedenti come quello di Matthew Landrus, produca deformazioni progressive analoghe a quelle già rilevate nell’ Adorazione ; sostituendo tale ipotesi con una struttura modulare unitaria, il dipinto si lascia invece ricostruire come un prisma stereometrico armonizzato da ritmi 1:4:1, 2:1:2 e 1:6. La sala dipinta non è più soltanto prospetticamente corretta: diventa una macchina visiva immersiva, inserita con minimi aggiustamenti nello spazio reale del refettorio e organizzata come una partitura architettonica governata da un unico modulo generatore. 
 Uno degli apporti più originali del corpus consiste nell’aver messo al centro non soltanto la misurabilità dello spazio, ma la sua rimontabilità. Le opere analizzate contengono, secondo questa ipotesi, le istruzioni per la propria ricostruzione: i “righelli di Leonardo” non servono solo al ricercatore contemporaneo per misurare il dipinto, ma appartengono al processo stesso con cui Leonardo ha generato lo spazio raffigurato. Da qui deriva una nozione forte di pittura come progetto: non superficie da decifrare simbolicamente in prima istanza, ma dispositivo costruttivo che rende verificabile la propria architettura interna. 
 Il contributo teorico complessivo del trittico consiste quindi nello spostare l’attenzione dalla prospettiva come codice astratto alla prospettiva come grammatica operativa, adattiva e incarnata. Leonardo appare come un autore che commisura la struttura geometrica alle esigenze narrative, alla posizione del corpo umano, alla funzione percettiva dell’orizzonte e alla continuità tra spazio dipinto e spazio reale. In questo senso, il corpus restituisce all’opera leonardesca una dimensione progettuale radicale: la pittura come simulatore spaziale, l’immagine come ambiente costruibile, la composizione come sintassi metrica in evoluzione. 
 Extended abstract (EN) 
 This corpus —  Leonardo's CAD, Leonardo's Rulers, Leonardo's Score  — advances a unified interpretation of three studies that originated independently yet converge on the same claim: Leonardo da Vinci neither applied Albertian square-grid perspective mechanically nor departed from it only through occasional anomalies, but progressively developed a personal metric-modular spatial grammar that can be reconstructed from the internal evidence of the works themselves. The inquiry is deliberately circumscribed: rather than offering a total interpretation of the paintings, it focuses on their reconstructible spaces and on the perspectival, metric, and modular structures that can be tested through reverse geometric analysis. 
 The corpus is organized as a developmental sequence. The  Annunciation  is read as the prototype of an inserted geometry based on visible metric cues; the preparatory drawing for the  Adoration of the Magi  reveals a generative 4:3 grid anchored to the Florentine  braccio ; and the  Last Supper  becomes the mature stage of a fully rhythmic and stereometric architecture governed by a single generative module. Taken together, the three case studies suggest not the repetition of a fixed formula, but the evolution of a spatial syntax that becomes progressively more complex, immersive, and internally harmonized. 
 Methodologically, the corpus is grounded in what the author calls the “Aristotelian obvious”: only what is visible, measurable, and geometrically accountable within the image is allowed to function as evidence. CAD reverse-engineering, inverse geometry, direct visual observation, and anthropometric as well as zoometric verification are combined in order to test whether the represented spaces are structurally coherent under alternative interpretative hypotheses. In this framework, details such as rusticated blocks, tiles, arcades, stairways, tapestries, and coffers are treated not as ornamental accessories but as operative rulers embedded in the pictorial field. 
 In the  Annunciation , the niche surrounding the Virgin is interpreted as a measurable spatial box structured by the module q, identified as half a Florentine  braccio . The visible ashlar pattern and floor tiling define a complete orthogonal reference system, allowing the reconstruction of depth, width, door opening, picture-plane distance, and horizon height. Crucially, the Virgin’s body is not simply placed within this space; it provides the anthropometric key for scaling it, so that the horizon line at approximately 3q corresponds to Mary’s seated shoulder height and turns the niche into a humanly calibrated environment rather than a generic backdrop. 
 In the  Adoration of the Magi , the study challenges the traditional assumption of a square perspective grid. The proposed 4:3 rectangular grid, tied to the Florentine  braccio , is said to restore geometric coherence to the full-centred arches and to resolve distortions previously interpreted as perspectival inaccuracies. At the same time, the stair system reveals the insertion of golden-triangle geometry and pentagonal proportional logic, producing a hybrid structure in which rational construction and harmonic elevation are mutually integrated 
 In the  Last Supper , the corpus extends this analytical framework to a more complex architectural environment. Against square-grid interpretations, including the well-known study by Matthew Landrus discussed in the document, the author argues for a unitary modular system governing the represented refectory through rhythmic ratios such as 1:4:1, 2:1:2, and 1:6. The resulting space is described as a stereometric prism harmonized across all three dimensions and inserted, with minimal adjustments, into the physical architecture of Santa Maria delle Grazie. 
 A major contribution of the corpus lies in redefining pictorial perspective as reassemblable architecture. The paintings are treated as if they contained the instructions for their own reconstruction: Leonardo’s “rulers” are not merely analytical tools used by the modern scholar, but traces of the original design procedure left visible within the image. This shift from measurable space to reassemblable space is central to the argument, because it transforms the painting from a surface to be interpreted into a constructive device whose internal logic can be experimentally verified. 
 The broader implication of the corpus is that Leonardo should be understood not only as a painter deploying perspective, but as an engineer of vision who adapts geometry to perception, narrative function, anthropometric scale, and architectural plausibility. The trilogy therefore proposes a substantial repositioning of Leonardo’s pictorial practice: perspective is no longer an abstract codified system applied to representation, but an evolving operational grammar through which painting becomes spatial simulation and visible form becomes constructible space. 
 Postfazione (it) 
 Collocato nel quadro degli studi su Leonardo, il corpus si distingue anzitutto per il tipo di domanda che pone. Molta letteratura precedente sull’ Annunciazione , sull’ Adorazione dei Magi  e sul  Cenacolo  si è concentrata su problemi di composizione, iconografia, simbolismo, qualità pittoriche, prospettiva intesa come impianto frontale o presunte anomalie rispetto a una norma albertiana data per acquisita; il presente trittico, invece, sposta il baricentro verso la ricostruibilità metrica degli spazi e verso la funzione operativa degli elementi dipinti. In questo senso, più che negare gli studi precedenti, il corpus ne modifica il fuoco epistemologico: dalla descrizione della forma alla verifica del procedimento costruttivo. 
 Per quanto riguarda l’ Annunciazione , il confronto più produttivo è con gli studi citati nel documento stesso: Carlo Pedretti, Antonio Natali, Roberto Bellucci e Franca Manenti Valli. Pedretti e Natali sono richiamati come interpreti delle apparenti anomalie prospettiche in chiave di visione laterale e anamorfica, mentre Bellucci viene riconosciuto per la ricostruzione dell’underdrawing e della griglia prospettica; il corpus si innesta su questa linea ma sostiene che la questione della sproporzione tra figure e architettura resti aperta finché non si assuma la nicchia come spazio modulare effettivamente misurabile. Nei confronti di Manenti Valli, il rapporto è esplicitamente dichiarato come complementare: la sua analisi proporzionale e armonica, fondata sul rettangolo √5, sulla serie di Fibonacci e sui rapporti musicali pitagorici, viene accolta come lettura rigorosa della superficie pittorica; il nuovo studio, però, rivendica un ulteriore passaggio, dalla geometria bidimensionale della composizione alla geometria tridimensionale dello spazio costruibile. 
 Questo slittamento metodologico è importante perché chiarisce la specificità del corpus. Laddove una parte della critica tende a leggere l’opera come deposito di valori simbolici, consonanze numeriche o libertà compositive rispetto alla norma, il trittico cerca una prova falsificabile nella coerenza metrica dell’architettura dipinta. L’idea non è che le letture simboliche siano errate, ma che esse non esauriscano la struttura dell’opera e che debbano essere integrate da una verifica geometrica capace di distinguere tra effetto figurativo e dispositivo costruttivo. 
 Nel caso dell’ Adorazione dei Magi , il corpus si misura con la tradizione che ha assunto la maglia quadrata come base del sistema prospettico del foglio 436 E. In particolare, il documento menziona lo studio di Fabrizio Ivan Apollonio e Riccardo Foschi come riferimento sul tema, ma propone un ribaltamento: le deformazioni riscontrate nelle arcate non sarebbero errori leonardeschi, bensì artefatti prodotti da un’ipotesi di partenza inadeguata. L’introduzione della maglia 4:3, unita al richiamo al braccio fiorentino e all’innesto della geometria pentagonale e aurea, permette al corpus di presentarsi non come pura revisione terminologica, ma come sostituzione di paradigma analitico. 
 La distanza dai precedenti studi, tuttavia, non consiste solo nella proposta di una nuova griglia. Consiste anche nel modo in cui tale griglia viene giustificata: non attraverso un sistema teorico imposto dall’esterno, ma attraverso una sequenza di osservazioni visive, verifiche inverse e controlli CAD che aspirano a convergere indipendentemente. È qui che il corpus rivendica il proprio tratto più originale: la critica dell’assioma iniziale. Se cambia l’assunto geometrico, cambiano anche gli errori attribuiti a Leonardo. 
 Sul  Cenacolo , il confronto è ancora più netto. Il documento cita esplicitamente Matthew Landrus come studio di riferimento fondato sulla maglia quadrata e affianca a questo contesto anche Tomás García-Salgado e Raphaël Mouterde, mentre la propria analisi si presenta come correzione metodologica di tale quadro. La tesi centrale è che le deformazioni degli arazzi e di altri elementi architettonici non attestino un’imprecisione del dipinto, ma derivino ancora una volta da una cattiva ipotesi ricostruttiva; adottando invece un modulo unitario e ritmi tridimensionali armonizzati, il  Cenacolo  si lascia leggere come un organismo stereometrico coerente. 
 Rispetto alla storiografia tradizionale, il corpus introduce anche una ridefinizione del rapporto tra pittura e architettura. In molti studi precedenti la prospettiva è trattata come mezzo di rappresentazione dello spazio; qui, invece, la pittura viene interpretata come simulatore spaziale e quasi come progetto esecutivo, nel quale l’architettura non è raffigurata soltanto per essere vista, ma per essere misurata e, in senso forte, rimontata. Questa idea produce un cambio di statuto critico: Leonardo non è più solo il pittore che padroneggia la profondità, ma il progettista che lascia nell’immagine tracce operative del proprio processo costruttivo. 
 Anche il rapporto con la tradizione teorica rinascimentale viene ridefinito. Alberti resta il punto di partenza storico inevitabile, e il documento riconosce apertamente che Leonardo ne conosce i principi; tuttavia, il corpus insiste sul fatto che il vinciano non si limiti a personalizzare la regola, ma elabori un sistema più autonomo, adattivo e commisurato alle esigenze della scena, della percezione e della scala umana. Il riferimento a Pacioli e alla  Divina proportione , insieme ai richiami alla geometria pentagonale e ai solidi, non serve qui a fondare un’esegesi esoterica, ma a storicizzare l’orizzonte tecnico e matematico entro cui le soluzioni leonardesche possono essere comprese. 
 Il corpus mostra infine una forte consonanza con alcune linee contemporanee di ricerca digital humanities, visual studies e technical art history, pur mantenendo una fisionomia autonoma. L’uso del CAD non è decorativo né illustrativo, ma funziona come banco di prova capace di confermare o smentire un’ipotesi; in questo, il lavoro si inserisce nel più ampio passaggio da una storia dell’arte puramente descrittiva a una storia dell’arte verificativa, sperimentale e replicabile. È probabilmente questo il suo apporto più rilevante rispetto agli studi precedenti sugli stessi argomenti: non solo una nuova interpretazione di tre opere, ma una proposta di metodo che invita a riconsiderare l’intera questione della prospettiva leonardesca in termini di evidenza, controllo e ricostruzione. 
   
 Afterword (en) 
 Placed within the field of Leonardo studies, this corpus is distinguished first of all by the question it asks. Much previous scholarship on the  Annunciation , the  Adoration of the Magi , and the  Last Supper  has concentrated on compositional issues, iconography, symbolism, pictorial qualities, perspective understood as a frontal system, or supposed anomalies measured against an assumed Albertian norm; this trilogy instead shifts the focus towards the metric reconstructibility of pictorial space and the operative function of painted elements. Rather than rejecting earlier studies, the corpus changes their epistemological focus: from describing form to testing the constructive procedure. 
 With regard to the  Annunciation , the most productive comparison is with the scholars expressly discussed in the text itself: Carlo Pedretti, Antonio Natali, Roberto Bellucci, and Franca Manenti Valli. Pedretti and Natali are recalled for interpreting apparent perspectival anomalies through lateral viewing and anamorphic effects, while Bellucci is acknowledged for his reconstruction of the underdrawing and the perspectival grid; the present corpus builds on this line of inquiry, but argues that the perceived disproportion between figures and architecture remains unresolved until the niche is treated as a genuinely measurable modular space. 
 The relationship with Manenti Valli is explicitly one of complementarity. Her analysis of proportional and harmonic structure—centred on the √5 rectangle, the Fibonacci sequence, and Pythagorean musical ratios—is recognised as a rigorous examination of the painting’s planar composition; the present study claims a further step, from the two-dimensional geometry of pictorial composition to the three-dimensional geometry of constructible space. Where Manenti Valli reads the corner blocks as bearers of numerical and symbolic meaning, this corpus treats them as operative metric instruments—rulers inserted into the scene in order to construct and control perspectival depth. The two approaches do not exclude one another: they answer different questions about the same work. 
 This methodological shift defines the specificity of the trilogy. Whereas part of the literature reads the work primarily as a repository of symbolic values, numerical consonances, or compositional freedoms in relation to established rules, the corpus seeks falsifiable evidence in the metric coherence of the painted architecture. The argument is not that symbolic readings are invalid, but that they do not exhaust the work’s structure and should be complemented by geometric testing able to distinguish a visual effect from a constructive device. 
 In the case of the  Adoration of the Magi , the corpus confronts the tradition that assumes a square grid as the basis of the perspectival system in Uffizi drawing 436 E. The document refers in particular to the study by Fabrizio Ivan Apollonio and Riccardo Foschi, but proposes a reversal: the distortions observed in the arcades are not Leonardesque errors, but artifacts generated by an inadequate initial hypothesis. The introduction of a 4:3 grid, combined with the Florentine  braccio  and the insertion of pentagonal and golden-ratio geometry, allows the study to advance not merely a terminological revision but a replacement of the analytical paradigm. 
 The distance from previous studies, however, does not lie only in proposing a different grid. It also lies in the way that grid is justified: not through a theoretical system imposed from outside, but through converging sequences of visual observation, inverse reconstruction, and CAD-based verification. Here the corpus asserts its most original feature: the critique of the initial axiom. If the geometrical assumption changes, the very errors attributed to Leonardo change as well. 
 The comparison is sharper still in the case of the  Last Supper . The text explicitly cites Matthew Landrus as a reference for a square-grid approach, alongside Tomás García-Salgado and Raphaël Mouterde, while presenting its own analysis as a methodological correction to that framework. Its central argument is that distortions in the tapestries and other architectural components do not demonstrate inaccuracies in the painting; rather, they once again arise from an incorrect reconstructive premise. Once a unitary module and harmonised three-dimensional rhythms are adopted, the  Last Supper  can instead be read as a coherent stereometric organism. 
 Compared with traditional historiography, the corpus also redefines the relationship between painting and architecture. In many earlier studies, perspective is treated as a means of representing space; here, painting is understood as a spatial simulator and almost as an executable project, in which architecture is depicted not only to be seen, but to be measured and, in a strong sense, reassembled. This changes the critical status of Leonardo: he is no longer only the painter who masters depth, but the designer who leaves operative traces of his constructive process visible within the image. 
 The relationship with Renaissance theory is consequently recast as well. Alberti remains the unavoidable historical point of departure, and the corpus openly acknowledges Leonardo’s knowledge of Albertian principles; nevertheless, it argues that Leonardo does not merely personalise the rule, but develops a more autonomous and adaptive system, calibrated to the requirements of the scene, perception, and human scale. References to Pacioli’s  Divina proportione , together with pentagonal geometry and the solids, do not serve here to support an esoteric reading; rather, they situate Leonardo’s solutions within their technical and mathematical horizon. 
 Finally, the corpus shows a strong affinity with contemporary strands of digital humanities, visual studies, and technical art history, while preserving a distinct identity. CAD is not used decoratively or illustratively, but as a testing ground capable of confirming or falsifying an hypothesis; in this respect, the work belongs to the broader movement from a purely descriptive art history towards a verificatory, experimental, and replicable art history. This is probably its most significant contribution in relation to previous studies on the same subjects: not only a new interpretation of three works, but a methodological proposal that invites a reconsideration of Leonardo’s perspective in terms of evidence, control, and reconstruction. 
   
   Nota metodologica e genesi del corpus    
    Leonardo’s Spatial Grammar: A CAD Reverse-Engineering Analysis - Leonardo's CAD, Leonardo's Rulers, Leonardo's Score    
       
   Leonardo’s CAD – Leonardo’s Rulers – Leonardo’s Score    riunisce tre studi nati da successive indagini sulla costruzione dello spazio nelle opere di Leonardo da Vinci: l’ Adorazione dei Magi , l’ Ultima Cena  e, retrospettivamente, l’ Annunciazione .  
  Il corpus non nasce da un programma di ricerca predefinito né dall’applicazione di un unico modello geometrico alle tre opere. Esso si è sviluppato progressivamente a partire da problemi specifici posti dalle opere stesse e dal confronto critico con precedenti ricostruzioni prospettiche. In ciascun caso, la ricerca ha cercato una risposta alternativa partendo non da un sistema teorico da sovrapporre all’immagine, ma dalle  tracce geometriche effettivamente visibili e misurabili .  
  La metodologia che emerge nel corso delle tre indagini è tuttavia la stessa: individuare elementi ricorrenti o strutturalmente significativi, assumerli come riferimenti metrici, formulare un’ipotesi sulla costruzione dello spazio e sottoporla a verifica mediante  ricostruzione geometrica inversa e CAD . Il modello non viene quindi imposto all’opera: è l’opera a fornire progressivamente gli indizi attraverso i quali il modello può essere ricostruito, verificato o eventualmente respinto.  
  In  Leonardo’s CAD , l’analisi della tavola 436 E dell’ Adorazione dei Magi  prende avvio dalla necessità di verificare criticamente l’interpretazione prospettica allora proposta da Apollonio e Foschi. La restituzione geometrica delle arcate conduce a un sistema modulare alternativo alla tradizionale griglia quadrata.  
  In  Leonardo’s Score , la stessa esigenza di verifica viene trasferita allo spazio dell’ Ultima Cena . L’attenzione si sposta dagli elementi curvi ai ritmi ripetuti di pareti, arazzi, travi e cassettoni, facendo emergere una grammatica modulare tridimensionale nella quale rapporti semplici e coordinati organizzano l’intero spazio rappresentato.  
  È proprio questa seconda indagine a generare la domanda successiva:  se Leonardo lasciava nei dipinti elementi capaci di misurare lo spazio rappresentato, potevano esistere strumenti analoghi già nelle opere giovanili?  Da questa domanda nasce  Leonardo’s Rulers , dedicato all’ Annunciazione . Qui le mattonelle e i bugnati della nicchia vengono osservati come  “righelli inseriti” nella scena : unità modulari che consentono di ricostruire uno spazio misurabile, calibrato sulla scala umana.  
  Considerati insieme, i tre studi rivelano così una continuità che non era stata postulata all’inizio della ricerca, ma è emersa dal confronto dei risultati. Dalla  geometria inserita  dell’ Annunciazione , attraverso la  geometria svelata  dell’ Adorazione , fino alla  geometria intonata  dell’ Ultima Cena , si delinea progressivamente un modo coerente di costruire e controllare lo spazio attraverso moduli, proporzioni, ritmo e prospettiva.  
  Il valore del corpus risiede quindi non soltanto nei singoli modelli ricostruttivi, ma nel fatto che  la metodologia comune emerge dai risultati anziché precederli . Le tre opere non vengono utilizzate per confermare una teoria preesistente: è la convergenza delle loro tracce geometriche, analizzate attraverso lo stesso procedimento di osservazione, misura, ipotesi e verifica, a suggerire l'esistenza di una grammatica spaziale coerente.  
  Il CAD assume in questo percorso una funzione precisa: non semplice strumento di visualizzazione, ma  strumento di verifica  capace anche di mettere alla prova e, se necessario, falsificare l’ipotesi ricostruttiva.  
  Il corpus propone infine una lettura di Leonardo nella quale la prospettiva non è soltanto una tecnica di rappresentazione, ma uno strumento progressivamente trasformato in  linguaggio architettonico : un linguaggio capace di misurare, costruire e accordare lo spazio. Uno spazio non soltanto rappresentato, ma  ricostruibile .

   Leonardo’s CAD – Leonardo’s Rulers – Leonardo’s Score    brings together three studies that emerged from successive investigations into the construction of space in Leonardo da Vinci’s works: the  Adoration of the Magi , the  Last Supper , and, retrospectively, the  Annunciation .  
  The corpus did not originate as a predefined research programme, nor from the application of a single geometric model to three works. It developed progressively from specific problems posed by the works themselves and from critical engagement with previous perspectival reconstructions. In each case, the investigation sought an alternative answer by starting not from a theoretical system imposed upon the image, but from the  geometric traces actually visible and measurable within it .  
  The methodology that emerges across the three investigations is nevertheless the same: identifying recurring or structurally significant elements, treating them as metric references, formulating a hypothesis concerning the construction of space, and testing it through  inverse geometric reconstruction and CAD . The model is therefore not imposed upon the work; rather, the work progressively provides the clues from which the model can be reconstructed, tested, or potentially rejected.  
  In  Leonardo’s CAD , the analysis of Uffizi sheet 436 E from the  Adoration of the Magi  began with the need to critically examine the perspectival interpretation proposed by Apollonio and Foschi. The geometric restitution of the arches led to a modular system alternative to the traditional square-based grid.  
  In  Leonardo’s Score , the same need for verification was transferred to the architectural space of the  Last Supper . Attention shifted from curved elements to the recurring rhythms of the walls, tapestries, beams and coffers, revealing a three-dimensional modular grammar in which simple, coordinated ratios organise the represented space.  
  This second investigation generated the next question:  if Leonardo left elements within his paintings capable of measuring represented space, could analogous instruments already be present in his earlier works?  This question led to  Leonardo’s Rulers , devoted to the  Annunciation . Here, the floor tiles and ashlar blocks of the niche are examined as  “rulers inserted into the scene” : modular units through which a measurable, human-scaled space can be reconstructed.  
  Considered together, the three studies therefore reveal a continuity that was not postulated at the outset, but emerged from the comparison of their results. From the  inserted geometry  of the  Annunciation , through the  revealed geometry  of the  Adoration , to the  intoned geometry  of the  Last Supper , a coherent way of constructing and controlling space through modules, proportions, rhythm and perspective progressively becomes visible.  
  The significance of the corpus therefore lies not only in its individual reconstructions, but in the fact that  the common methodology emerges from the results rather than preceding them . The three works are not used to confirm a pre-existing theory: it is the convergence of their geometric traces, investigated through the same sequence of observation, measurement, hypothesis and verification, that suggests the existence of a coherent spatial grammar.  
  Within this process, CAD has a precise function: not merely a tool for visualisation, but a  means of verification  capable of testing and, where necessary, falsifying the proposed reconstruction.  
  The corpus ultimately proposes a reading of Leonardo in which perspective is not merely a technique of representation, but a progressively developed  architectural language : a language capable of measuring, constructing and tuning space.   Space that is not merely represented, but  reconstructable .  
     
   Giancarlo De Leo

title: The Impact of Employee Motivation on Productivity and Organizational Performance in Laguna Small and Medium Enterprises
journal: Rochelle Mae Berbon, Zyra Joy Defante, Hannah Nicole Galang
text: The Impact of Employee Motivation on Productivity and Organizational Performance in Laguna Small and Medium Enterprises.  Resiliency and long-term sustainability of small and medium enterprises (SMEs) heavily rely on effective workforce and employee engagement. However, localized operational gap persists regarding how distinct intrinsic and extrinsic motivational dimensions affect workforce outcomes, leaving it unclear which drivers exert the most critical influence on productivity and organizational performance within this developing regional economy. This study examines the relationship between employee motivation, productivity, and organizational performance among Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) in Laguna, Philippines. Utilizing a quantitative, descriptive-correlational research design, data was gathered through a structured 5-point Likert scale questionnaire from respondents operating across key functional departments. Respondents are employees working in selected Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) in Laguna. The statistical analysis revealed that both intrinsic and extrinsic motivation are exceptionally high among employees. Employees exhibit their highest drive when experiencing a sense of personal accomplishment, having opportunities to learn and grow, and taking pride in the quality of their work. While financial compensation remains a vital factor, salary received the lowest relative rating among the external indicators, suggesting that monetary reward alone is insufficient for sustaining long-term engagement. In terms of organizational outcomes, overall employee performance is highly rated, marked by strong execution in attendance, punctuality, efficiency, and the quality of work output. However, employees showed the least inclination toward assuming additional responsibilities, indicating a critical area where employers must provide further encouragement, recognition, and support to foster proactive participation. Statistical analyses confirm that as employee motivation increases, performance increases accordingly. Both motivational dimensions share a significant positive relationship with performance, but intrinsic motivation possesses a much stronger connection than extrinsic motivation. In conclusion, Employee motivation plays a critical role in driving productivity and overall organizational performance within Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) in Laguna. While workforce performance is generally high particularly regarding attendance, efficiency, and quality of output, there remains a notable reluctance among employees to assume additional responsibilities, highlighting a need for enhanced institutional support, recognition, and targeted encouragement. Intrinsic motivation, derived from personal growth, autonomy, and a sense of accomplishment, serves as the primary factor for exceptional employee performance. Additionally, extrinsic factors such as financial incentives and benefits, while essential, act predominantly as supportive mechanisms rather than primary drivers. Therefore, to ensure long-term business sustainability and optimal productivity, small and medium enterprises (SMEs) must transition from a heavy reliance on financial incentives toward fostering an organizational culture that prioritizes meaningful work, professional development, and employee involvement.

title: Dataset: Turbulence flux-variance scaling and anisotropy parameters from a mountain observatory for evaluating Monin-Obukhov Similarity Theory (MOST)
journal: Zhang, Yan, Cheng, Xueling, Zhang, Keyu
text:
Dataset: Turbulence flux-variance scaling and anisotropy parameters from a mountain observatory for evaluating Monin-Obukhov Similarity Theory (MOST).   This dataset contains high-temporal-resolution atmospheric turbulence and flux measurements collected during the ABLES-MOST (Atmospheric Boundary Layer Experimental Study – Micrometeorological Observational and Scaling Techniques) field campaign. The data span a continuous observational period from  April 2024 to  March 2025, with a temporal resolution of 30 minutes. All measurements were obtained at a constant height of 7.3 m above ground level using eddy-covariance instrumentation, including a sonic anemometer and gas analyzers (IRGASON, Campbell Scientific Inc., USA). 
 Key measured and derived variables include: - Steady State tests: momentum flux (SST_uw) , sensible heat flux (SST_wTs), latent heat flux (SST_wH2O), and CO₂ flux (SST_wCO2) - Turbulence statistics: standard deviations of three-dimensional wind components (u_std, v_std, w_std), sonic temperature (Ts_std), specific humidity (q_std), and CO₂ concentration (c_std) - Scaling parameters: friction velocity (ustar), temperature scale (tstar), humidity scale (qstar), CO₂ scale (cstar), and Obukhov length (L) - Meteorological conditions: mean horizontal wind speed (U_mean) and wind direction (WD) - Additional diagnostic variables: anisotropy parameter (aniso_beta, xB and yB) 
 The dataset is structured in comma-separated format with clear column headers and consistent timestamp formatting. It is suitable for investigating surface-layer similarity theory, validating flux–variance scaling relationships, assessing turbulence characteristics under varying stability conditions, and supporting boundary-layer parameterization in numerical models. Potential applications include micrometeorological research, land–atmosphere interaction studies, carbon cycle analysis, and environmental monitoring. 
 Users are advised to perform appropriate quality control (e.g., stationarity tests, outlier filtering) .

title: MercaderLabAnatomy/napari-tmidas: v0.5.13
text:
MercaderLabAnatomy/napari-tmidas: v0.5.13.  Performance — memory & streaming 
 
    65a16a7  perf(labels): stream remove-small and merge-small so huge stacks stop OOM-killing 
"Remove Small Labels" and "Merge Small Labels to Neighbors" were OOM-killing
napari on 4D label images (~90 MB compressed, 52–73 GB dense). Both now set
 skip_load=True  and do their own streamed I/O. Remove-small goes plane by
plane: pass 1 accumulates per-label counts with  np.bincount , pass 2 applies
a LUT straight into  TiffWriter  — peak RSS 1.01 GB on a 52 GB file. Merging
is spatial, so it streams block by block through a single reused volume
buffer, merged in place (5.92 GB → 2.61 GB, 138 s → 97 s). Also fixed
 np.bincount  upcasting whole uint32 volumes to int64. Output verified
byte-identical to the in-memory paths; 22 tests added. 
 
    213995e  perf: keep large inputs lazy end to end so peak stops tracking the stack 
The worker densified every lazy input for any function without a
 _source_filepath  parameter, so 30 of 39 audited functions had peak growing
~2.0x with the input. New  @chunked  decorator maps existing NumPy bodies
over blocks of a lazy Dask input, cutting only leading axes so a body always
sees whole planes or volumes — byte-identical results, no halo, no
re-tuning. TIFFs over 2 GB now open page-wise as Dask; a lazy result above
the stream budget is written block by block instead of computed into RAM.
CLAHE gets a  max_dask_workers  ceiling (it peaks at ~28x its block in
float64), holding at ~3.8 GB regardless of input size. 
 
    a3c8cd7  perf(convpaint): segment time series per timepoint across GPUs instead of whole 
The old path densified the entire input and pre-allocated the full uint32
output beside it — 26 GB plus 52 GB committed before a single timepoint was
touched. Timepoints are now segmented one at a time and written straight to
disk (0.8 GB in, 1.7 GB out each), staged through an on-disk Zarr scratch
store on the output filesystem. New  n_workers  parameter runs that many
timepoints concurrently, each pinned round-robin to a visible CUDA device. 
 
    f05f4d0  fix(streaming): cap tifffile compression workers so writes stop buffering the whole output 
tifffile's threaded compression drains the plane iterator with no
backpressure, so peak scaled with the whole output — 545 MB vs 3 MB on a
48-block zlib write.  maxworkers=1  applied to all three streaming writers. 
 
 
 Refactor 
 
   af48d30  refactor: extract one streamed-TIFF writer and drop the dead zarr v2 paths 
Four call sites had grown their own copy of the same streamed
 TiffWriter.write()  block; they now share
 ome_output_utils.stream_planes_to_tiff , with the two kwargs that make it
correct ( photometric="minisblack" ,  maxworkers=1 ) explained once. The
zarr v2 write branches are gone — the package requires zarr>=3, so they
could only produce output older than anything able to run the code. Reading
v2 is untouched. 
 
 Fixes 
 
    b263365  fix: three latent bugs in monkeypatching, rolling ball, and zarr label pairing 
Re-importing  basic.py  or  file_compression.py  re-wrapped an
already-wrapped  ProcessingWorker.process_file , making every call recurse
until the stack ran out. Rolling ball spanned every axis it was handed, so a
TZYX stack rolled a four-dimensional ball (101**4 kernel = 832 MB, 25 min at
13.7 GB RSS on a 5 MB stack) — and blended background across timepoints and
channels; it now works one YX plane at a time, as ImageJ does. A duplicated
extension list omitted  .zarr , so Zarr label files could never be paired. 
 
    d6d52af  fix: survive napari-ome-zarr 0.10 rejecting sources without coordinate transforms 
0.10 dereferences the affine built from  coordinateTransformations 
unguarded, raising  AttributeError  where 0.8 returned identity.
 AttributeError  was not caught by the four fallback handlers, so older
acquisitions that omit those transforms hard-failed instead of falling back
to the basic zarr reader, which loads them fine. 
 
 
 Tests 
 
   44e38ac  test(merge-small-labels): bound peak by block multiple, not block plus constant 
Test-only. The "one block + a constant" bound assumed scipy's transient
working room was fixed; it drifts 9.3 → 15.6 MB and varies with interpreter
version, and py3.11 CI crossed it. Now bounded by a multiple of the block,
which is the shape of the regression being defended against.

title: Depth Curated Open-Ocean Fish Records from iDigBio
text:
Depth Curated Open-Ocean Fish Records from iDigBio.  Overview 
 Our raw data were sourced from the Integrated Digitized Biocollections portal (iDigBio), a U.S. National Science Foundation-funded repository for the Advancing Digitization of Biodiversity Collections (ADBC) program. iDigBio houses millions of specimen records and digitized images from hundreds of U.S. based natural history collections representing taxa from throughout the tree of life. iDigBio searches return both verbatim records and records that have been harmonzied and simplified to include only simple, commonly-used text fields. For our purposes, we wanted geographic coordinates (i.e. latitude and longitude) and the verbatim depth field to complete missing depths for as many records as possible; therefore, we chose to use the raw results of our query, below, as the basis for custom harmonization. 
 Data extraction from iDigBio 
 Database query 
 A query (below) was constructed in the  iDigBio portal  using Class-> Actinopterygii and excluded all freshwater results. The resulting search returned 2,984,839 raw records. Data were downloaded as .csv files.  
 {"core_type": "records", "rq": {"family": {"type": "exists"}, "locality": {"type": "exists"}, "geopoint": {"type": "exists"}, "basisofrecord": "PreservedSpecimen", "scientificname": {"type": "exists"}, "catalognumber": {"type": "exists"}, "class": "Actinopterygii"}, "form": "dwca-csv", "core_source": "indexterms", "mediarecord_fields": null, "record_fields": null, "mq": null} 
 Museums providing data 
 University of Florida, Florida Museum of Natural History (UF); Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County (LACM); Museum of Comparative Zoology, Harvard University (MCZ); Oregon State University (OS); Biodiversity Research and Teaching Collections, Department of Wildlife and Fisheries Sciences, Texas A&M University (TCWC); Yale University, Peabody Museum of Natural History (YPM) Smithsonian Institution, National Museum of Natural History (USNM); Colección Ictiológica del Centro Interdisciplinario de Ciencias Marinas, Instituto Politécnico Nacional (CICIMAR-IPN); Western Australian Museum (WAM); University of Kansas Biodiversity Institute (KU); South Australian Museum (SAMA); Colección Ictiológica del Instituto de Ciencias del Mar y Limnología, Unidad Mazatlán, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (ICMyL-UNAM); Commonwealth Scientific & Industrial Research Organization, National Research Collections Australia, Australian National Fish Collection (CSIRO); Museums Victoria (NMV); Colección Nacional de Peces, Instituto de Biología, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (IBUNAM); Scripps Institution of Oceanography, Marine Vertebrate Collection, University of California San Diego (SIO); Queensland Museum, Centre for Biodiversity (QM); Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle (MNHN); Dubrovnik Natural History Museum (ZMUC/NHMD); Field Museum of Natural History (FMNH); Université d'Antananarivo, Département de Biologie Animale (UA); Zoological Museum, I. Mechnikov Odessa National University (ZMO); The Bernice Pauahi Bishop Museum, Department of Zoology (BPBM); Alabama Museum of Natural History, The University of Alabama (UAM); Georgian National Museum (GNM); University of Colorado Museum of Natural History (UCM). 
   
 Data Processing 
 Taxonomic harmonization 
 Missing genus information was programmatically completed where possible based on provided binomial scientific names. Then, common misspellings were corrected, and manual inspection of taxonomic inconsistencies was performed to ensure alignment with Eschmeyer’s Catalog of Fishes16 (accessed 12 December 2023), including further misspellings and inconsistent family assignments. The resulting taxonomic names were further rectified against the World Register of Marine Species (WoRMS; marinespecies.org, accessed 27 August, 2026) taxonomic database to render our final dataset compatible with other large marine datasets, such as those provided by the Ocean Biodiversity Information System (OBIS; obis.org). Both taxonomies were retained to maximize compatibility for diverse use cases. 
 Depth extraction and standardization 
 To address formatting heterogeneity across raw fields (“minimumDepthInMeters”, “maximumDepthInMeters”, and “verbatimDepth”), depth information was standardized through a four-stage parsing pipeline across all three fields. First, strings lacking numeric digits (e.g., "shallow") were discarded. For remaining entries (e.g., "Start-end: 260-259 m", "20 FATHOMS"), numeric values and unit identifiers were extracted using regular expressions. Extracted units (centimeters, feet, inches, fathoms) were converted to meters. Unitless values were assumed to represent meters. Where two numeric values were present in a single entry, the smaller value was assigned to “minimumDepthInMeters” and the larger to “maximumDepthInMeters”. Single numeric values across all three fields were assigned to both “minimumDepthInMeters” and “minimumDepthInMeters”. Mean sampling depth (hereafter "depth") was calculated as the midpoint of these values (i.e. sum of “maximumDepthInMeters” and “minimumDepthInMeters” divided by two), and depth uncertainty was calculated as half the range of these values  (i.e. difference between “maximumDepthInMeters” and “minimumDepthInMeters” divided by two). Records without recoverable numeric depth data were removed prior to analysis. 
 Spatial filtering and bathymetric validation 
 Terrestrial records were removed using a global land mask derived from the Natural Earth dataset via the rnaturalearthdata R package13. Bathymetric consistency was evaluated using the ETOPO global relief model14. Records with reported maximum depth exceeding 99% of local bathymetric depth were excluded to reduce inconsistencies arising from georeferencing, transcription, or unit errors. 
 License and citation harmonization 
 iDigBio data are covered under a CC0 (public access) use license, but each individual organization carries its own level of coverage and attribution; only public facing records are shared in the portal, and thus, were included in our dataset. Use licenses from the raw dataset were provided via one of two fields, “dcterms.license” or “dc.rights”. We united these two fields into a single license field; only 48% of records had a specified license, all of which were versions of either CC0 or CC-BY. We also harmonized the dataset citation field, “dcterms.bibliographicCitation”, by stripping out individual specimen catalog numbers (which we supply as an unedited field populated directly from iDigBio in the final dataset), so that there is only one bibliographic citation per collection. In addition to supplying the harmonized citations in the final dataset, we now include these citations at the end of each markdown file on GitHub and in the Zenodo README file accompanying the final dataset.  
 Data Records 
 The final, curated dataset comprises 354,622 preserved specimen records representing more than 11,294 marine teleost fish species (59.2% of marine Actinopterygii species currently recognized by WoRMS). The final dataset we provide reflects the fully processed output following taxonomic harmonization, depth standardization, and bathymetric validation. Each row corresponds to a single vouchered specimen record and includes harmonized taxonomic fields, harmonized minimum and maximum depth (meters), extracted seafloor depth (meters), calculated mean depth and depth uncertainty (meters), and harmonized licenses and bibliographic citations, all derived as described above. We further provide the following fields as they were received from iDigBio to broaden potential use cases and ensure proper ability to trace records back to their originating specimens: iDigBio coreid, catalog number, dataset name, collection code, collection ID, institution code, latitude and longitude coordinates, coordinate uncertainty in meters, coordinate precision, collection date, basis of record, and sampling protocol.

title: Children Reimagining Mobility: A Participatory Toolbox for Schools, Cities and Policymakers
text:
Children Reimagining Mobility: A Participatory Toolbox for Schools, Cities and Policymakers.   Children Reimagining Mobility: A Participatory Toolbox for Schools, Cities and Policymakers  provides a practical participatory methodology for exploring how children experience everyday mobility and how their knowledge can contribute to more child-responsive urban environments. 
 Developed through doctoral research at Frederick University and informed by participatory workshops with children in Limassol, Cyprus, the toolbox combines guided discussion, questionnaires, drawing, collaborative model-making and children’s own explanations. The methodology supports the exploration of children’s travel patterns, emotional and physical experiences of journeys, perceptions of safety and accessibility, environmental barriers, and imagined alternatives for safer, healthier and more enjoyable mobility. 
 The toolbox is intended for teachers and schools, municipalities and local authorities, urban and transport planners, policymakers, researchers and universities, NGOs, and community organisations. It provides practical guidance on workshop preparation, ethics and safeguarding, implementation, documentation and interpretation, as well as a framework for translating children’s experiential knowledge into planning-relevant evidence. 
 The methodology recognises children as knowledgeable users of the city and provides structured, multimodal ways for their experiences and ideas to contribute to planning, education and policy.
