title: UK’s small power plants face continued cyber risk after Iran-linked hack
text: UK’s small power plants face continued cyber risk after Iran-linked hack. Hundreds of Britain’s smallest power plants could remain at a higher risk to state-sponsored cyber-attacks until the 2030s despite a successful Iran-linked hack last month, it has emerged. Officials this week briefed energy bosses on the breach, which is understood to have shut an unnamed small gas power plant for four days last month, and put the industry on alert over the growing cyber threat facing energy infrastructure. However, the government’s own plan to toughen the baseline cybersecurity standards for Britain’s smallest power generators will not be required until the end of 2030, raising concerns over “an unacceptable gamble with our national security”. Official government documents, published this month, call for the industry regulator, Ofgem, to lay out proposals for new baseline cyber resilience requirements for gas and electricity infrastructure by the end of 2027, ahead of implementing new standards by the end of 2030. The Guardian understands that the hack has not altered this timeline. The new requirements would cover the type of small-scale gas plant which is understood to have been successfully attacked by the Iran-linked hackers in the weeks before the government set out its timeline for bolstering the sector’s cybersecurity standards. Reports of the unprecedented cyber hack emerged as the Cabinet Office prepares to urge UK citizens to stock up on tinned food and bottled water to prepare for extreme weather events and potential attacks from hostile states. Calum Miller, the Lib Dems’ foreign affairs spokesperson, said: “Leaving hundreds of small power generators exposed to cyber threats until the 2030s is simply an unacceptable gamble with our national security.” Britain has hundreds of small-scale, unmanned gas plants connected to local power grids which are typically idle for most of the year but can be used to ramp up generation when electricity supplies are squeezed. Although the outage had no impact on the electricity system, the attack has raised concerns about vulnerabilities in locally connected power infrastructure which is not required to meet the same security standards as large-scale power plants and transmission assets. “The government should not have to wait for the lights to go out before taking the security of our energy infrastructure seriously,” Miller said. “They must immediately fast-track these regulations, not leave them until the 2030s. We mustn’t leave an open goal to hostile states at a time of heightened global threats.” The government opened a consultation into the cyber resilience of power generators in March, after it introduced the cyber security and resilience bill to parliament late last year, with a warning that the UK now faces four nationally significant cyber-attacks every week. Michael Shanks, the energy minister, said in the consultation that the UK “needs to keep pace with the current threat landscape”. An industry source familiar with the post-attack industry briefing confirmed reports, which first appeared in the Sunday Telegraph, that the plant was shut down for about four days in one the most successful cyber-attacks on UK energy infrastructure. “We should use it as a warning rather than wait for an incident,” according to Rafael Narezzi, chief executive of Centrii, an energy cybersecurity specialist. “Across the UK energy system we have small, medium and large generation assets, increasingly connected through digital systems, remote access, third parties and operational technology. This particular incident may not have had consequences for the wider grid, but the next one could be different.” “What concerns me about this incident is not necessarily the size of the power generator that was affected, but how many others may be out there,” Narezzi added. “Attackers do not necessarily select their targets according to how many megawatts they generate. They look for vulnerabilities, trusted access and opportunities. “The UK has thousands of distributed assets increasingly contributing to how our energy system operates. Individually, many may appear insignificant. Collectively, their resilience matters enormously.” A government spokesperson said: “The UK has a highly resilient energy system. We work closely with the energy sector to protect infrastructure and ensure the highest security standards. “We are alive to growing cybersecurity threats, which is why we also committed to reviewing the cyber resilience requirement for the downstream gas and electricity sector and are driving this work forward through parliament,” they added. Ofgem was also contacted for comment.

title: Vulnerable children deliberately self-harming to stay in care, research finds
text: Vulnerable children deliberately self-harming to stay in care, research finds. Some of the most vulnerable children and young people in care are deliberately self-harming to avoid being abandoned when they get better or turn 18 and face a “cliff edge” of no further support, according to research. Abi Booth, a psychotherapist who works with children and young people, said some were in a “catastrophic situation” in which they were hurting themselves to keep their place in therapeutic facilities. Booth said this group of young people believed the only way they could stay safe was not to “get better” from their mental health conditions and to become more ill by severely self-harming or attempting suicide. A government review into the deaths of 112 care leavers in England aged 18-24 in 2025 identified a dramatic drop in support at the age of 18. The Guardian revealed in April that there had been an almost fivefold increase in children in unregulated social care settings in England. Booth said: “Society’s system around the most vulnerable people in the UK is failing them at every level … Of the hundreds of young people I have spoken to in the course of my work in recent years, every single one has told me that the system is pushing them into patterns of risk. “Many of these children and young people have experienced extreme neglect and often physical and sexual abuse. Some are so badly scarred from self-harming there isn’t an inch of their bodies left untouched. They see self-harming as a route to safety. They are living in a state of terror, which may be hidden underneath layers of bravado.” Booth said that while not all children and young people in the care system fitted this description, she feared the number was growing, as indicated by the proliferation of private care units. There are 400,000 children in the social care system in England with nearly 84,000 looked after by local authorities. Booth said that paradoxically they saw self-harm as a route to safety because while they were undesirable to financially overstretched local authorities, they were a valuable commodity to private care companies. It was only by being high-risk that they could maintain their place in the care system. Councils often outsource these complex cases to private companies that can charge £20,000 or more per week per young person. Booth, who has carried out in-depth research into 12 children, said that while in inpatient psychiatric units, these children and young people were “learning the tricks of the trade” in terms of more severe and sophisticated methods of self-harming and suicide attempts. “These young people are a currency. They are more profitable the riskier they are,” Booth said. She is calling for change to better protect this group of young people without leaving them as “commodities” for the profit-driven private care companies. “I want to shine a light on the reality of life for these young people in the hope of inspiring some change,” she said. A report from parliament’s joint committee on human rights has found that the accommodation model in children’s social care is broken. The report, published on Thursday, found that a lack of capacity has resulted in children being placed in expensive and wholly inadequate accommodation, often far from support networks. It calls on government to end the use of unregulated spaces as a matter of urgency. It says measures that should be explored include increasing efforts to drive up local authority supply of placements through adequate funding, carrying out tougher inspections, and tackling delays in the registration process for homes. The chair of the joint committee, David Alton, said: “We have a moral duty as a society to uphold the human rights of children and young people. The children’s social care system is there to be a crucial safety net to support the most vulnerable in society. “The evidence we have heard from children in care, care leavers and experts in the field is that too often it is failing to prevent people falling through the gaps. The challenges for those in need of care do not stop when childhood ends – from the ‘cliff edge’ of support ending at the age of 18, to the increased likelihood of entering the criminal justice system, to facing discrimination once they leave care.” The Department for Education said the government is investing £25 million to help thousands more care leavers access homes with support attached and that steps are being taken to crack down on illegal and unregistered children’s homes. In the UK, the youth suicide charity Papyrus can be contacted on 0800 068 4141 or email pat@papyrus-uk.org , and in the UK and Ireland Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline is at 988 or chat for support. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

title: Liverpool agree £120m fee for Bradley Barcola after breakthrough talks with PSG
text: Liverpool agree £120m fee for Bradley Barcola after breakthrough talks with PSG. Liverpool are closing in on a £120m deal for Bradley Barcola following a breakthrough in talks with Paris Saint-Germain. Barcola has been Liverpool’s main transfer target all summer only for PSG’s £145m valuation to prove a significant hurdle. However, further negotiations on Thursday night ended in an outline agreement being reached over a compromise fee. Liverpool have agreed to pay a guaranteed sum of just over £100m for the France international, with add-ons based on individual and team success, taking the overall package to around £120m. The full structure of the deal has not been finalised but last night’s breakthrough, coupled with PSG’s willingness to lower their asking price for the 23-year-old, should see Barcola complete his move to Merseyside before Tuesday’s transfer deadline. Liverpool were informed last month that the player was keen to join them, having fallen down the pecking order for Luis Enrique’s team. Barcola has two years remaining on his PSG contract but informed the club that he will not be signing an extension. The two-time European champions have added Ferran Torres, Maghnes Akliouche and Mika Godts to their formidable attacking options this summer and subsequently omitted Barcola from their matchday squads this season. PSG signed Barcola for €45m from Lyon in 2023 and the winger has played a prominent role in the rise of Enrique’s Champions League winners. But Enrique’s preference for a front line of Désiré Doué, Ousmane Dembélé and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia in PSG’s biggest matches last season prompted Barcola to consider his options. The arrival of Barcola – and sources close to the deal insist it is not done yet – would make him potentially the second most expensive signing in Liverpool’s history behind £125m Alexander Isak, but the club have still to land a replacement for Mohamed Salah on the right. Liverpool have had two bids rejected by Brighton for Yankuba Minteh and, despite enquiring over Ismaïla Sarr’s availability, have not made an offer for the Crystal Palace forward.

title: Albanese vows refugee intake won’t be slashed after earlier reports of Coalition-level cut
text: Albanese vows refugee intake won’t be slashed after earlier reports of Coalition-level cut. Anthony Albanese has guaranteed Australia’s annual refugee intake will not be cut next financial year, shutting down plans for the arrivals quota to drop by one-third to Coalition-era levels. Labor MPs and refugee advocates reacted angrily to news on Thursday morning that the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, was planning to cut intake of 20,000 arrivals to 13,750 in 2027-28. By late afternoon, the prime minister confirmed the change would not proceed. News of the plan coincided with efforts by Labor to drive down migration levels amid increasing political pressure from One Nation . “The refugee intake needs to be renewed in the coming budget as the 20,000 places was available for 4 years,” Albanese said in a statement. “This intake number remains government policy and will be continued in future years, consistent with Australia’s humanitarian commitments and sits beside our strong border security measures.” Related: One Nation’s immigration policy is hard to define – even by its own MPs Migration settings are the subject of an internal fight within Labor, as the government seeks to bring net overseas migration down to 225,000 next financial year. Burke had delayed announcing the broader policy earlier this month. Rules for backpackers will be tightened, including working holidaymaker settings for Britons coming to Australia. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Earlier, when asked about the refugee intake changes on Thursday, Albanese hinted some of the reporting was incorrect and said Labor was responding to post-pandemic fluctuations. “We’re worried about trying to get numbers right,” the prime minister said at a regional summit in Dubbo. “We’re responding to national needs,” he said. “There is a current spike in the support for One Nation, quite clearly, but we’ve responded. We started lowering the numbers well before that occurred because we recognise that we want to get that right to assist the Australian economy.” In 2015, Labor’s national conference committed the party to accepting 27,000 refugees a year by 2025, part of a heated debate over asylum seeker policy and boat turnbacks. At the party’s most recent national conference , held in Adelaide in July, delegates approved language, saying: “Labor will seek, in the short term, to maintain Australia’s government funded humanitarian intake numbers at 20,000 places per year while also continuing to aspire to achieving 27,000 places per year.” Jana Favero, the Asylum Seeker Resource Centre’s deputy chief executive, said lowering the refugee intake would betray people around the world who were relying on Australia. “There are already Australian families desperately waiting to bring loved ones to safety from Iran, Sudan, Gaza and conflicts around the world,” she said. “What makes this even more disturbing is the politics behind it. The government appears increasingly willing to let One Nation dictate the terms of the migration debate, even when that means abandoning commitments made by its own party just weeks ago.” Paul Power, of the Refugee Council of Australia, said the proposed cut went against pledges made by the government at home and abroad. “When the Albanese government increased the refugee and humanitarian program to 20,000 places in 2023, there was no hint that this was a short-term increase. “Until now, Australia has been the only OECD country with a significant refugee resettlement program not to cut places in the past two years. Such a cut would make little difference to Australia’s net overseas migration but be devastating for people seeking a path to safety.” The Greens’ immigration spokesperson David Shoebridge said punishing vulnerable people was a backward step for the country. “The difference between One Nation and Labor is that, when One Nation attacks refugees, they don’t then pat themselves on the back for how much they support multiculturalism,” he said.

title: UK urged to help free British-Egyptian ‘arrested in Cairo over sister’s activism’
text: UK urged to help free British-Egyptian ‘arrested in Cairo over sister’s activism’. The UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release of a British-Egyptian woman who it is claimed has been arrested in Cairo because of her sister’s political activism. Eman el-Shazly, a 45-year-old based in Birmingham, was arrested on 16 August while visiting Egypt. Her lawyers say she has been detained in an attempt to silence her sister Mona, a relentless and harsh critic of the Egyptian government on her UK-based YouTube channel. Her two brothers have already spent three years in jail and, in May, were rearrested. They were previously held in pre-trial detention, facing charges of “promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation on social media, as well as broadcasting false news harmful to state security”. The UK Foreign Office has confirmed to the husband of Eman that she is being held in the Ramadan rehabilitation centre and her case has been given the same file number as that of her two brothers, Hassan and Eid. The government of President Abdel Fatah al-Sisi has faced allegations that it frequently arrests relatives of political critics to put indirect pressure on the dissidents to end their overseas criticism of his rule or of state corruption. Much of Mona’s activism focuses on alleged cases of corruption inside the security services or public utilities, a highly sensitive subject in Egypt. Arfan Rashid, the lawyer acting for Eman’s husband with whom she has four children, says that unlike Mona his wife has never been involved in politics, and had gone to Cairo two months ago to look after her ill mother after the arrest of her two brothers. “There is ample evidence that Eman has been arrested to silence Mona,” Rashid said. He added that Eman had told the security officials she was no longer in contact with her sister, and that many family members had repeatedly asked her to stop her political activism in the UK, but to no effect. Mona confirmed to the Guardian that she had been asked to halt her activism by other family members, including to take down her YouTube videos. But she added: “I have done nothing wrong nor broken any law … I am a very strong woman, but it is very traumatic for me since 11 or 12 children are without their parents. It is a horrible situation, but the Egyptian government will not stop if I appear weak. The government is close to collapsing.” Rashid said the UK government had recognised the practice of “punishment by proxy” in Egypt in its country profile policy and information note published in March 2026. Human Rights Watch and the House of Commons library warned in 2021 of an escalating pattern in which Egyptian family members of critics living abroad were being targeted. Mona runs a YouTube channel in the UK that has 130,000 subscribers. She is also active on X, making specific and controversial claims about government officials. The UK’s Foreign Office representation in Cairo has asked for access to see Eman but has not yet received a positive reply. Eman’s husband, Zeesharn Moustapha, has said Egyptian police and security officers attended the family home where she was staying a few days before the arrest, and demanded that Eman tell Mona to stop publishing material against the Egyptian government. On X, Mona has claimed as many as five members of her family have been detained or harassed by the Egyptian authorities. She wrote: “Kinship is something beyond my family’s will, and I invite them to disown me to save themselves from this despicable, illegitimate dictator. I am the one opposing Sisi, not five individuals from my family. This is a crime against humanity that does not lapse with time.” She has lived in the UK for 18 years. Eman became a British citizen through marriage. Her lawyer has asked whether Alistair Burt, the UK’s new envoy on complex consular cases, should be asked to intervene by the Foreign Office. Burt was appointed a month ago and has been tasked with working to secure the release of British citizens held abroad. Burt has already met Gurpreet Singh Johal, the brother of Jagtar Singh Johal, who has been detained by the Indian authorities for nearly nine years without a conviction. The Foreign Office has been approached for comment.

title: Ukraine’s drone attacks have left Russia desperately scrambling for oil imports
text: Ukraine’s drone attacks have left Russia desperately scrambling for oil imports. A sanctioned shadow fleet tanker carries oil from Nato member Turkey to a Russian Baltic port. A deal is signed for Russian oil to be processed in Kazakhstan. Fuel cargoes arrive from India via Egypt. The Kremlin pressures allies to sell it badly needed fuel. The data points may be diverse, but they point to a single inescapable conclusion. In the space of a summer, Russia, once the world’s second-largest producer of crude oil , has been plunged into a desperate scramble to find sources of gasoline to plug the ever-growing holes in its refining capacity. The Kremlin has tapped into a widening number of sources in recent weeks to alleviate an energy crisis that has led to rationing at filling stations, as long-range drone attacks from Ukraine target the oil processing plants that usually supply them. For the first time, Russia this week bought a shipment of 200,000 barrels of gasoline from Turkey, which are being shipped from Mersin to the Baltic port of Primorsk via a sanctioned tanker, the Wendrix. It is the fifth confirmed seaborne delivery of vehicle fuel this summer, after previous shipments via Egypt from a refinery at Vadinar in India, amounting to 1m barrels in total. Russia has also signed a deal with the Kondensat oil refinery in western Kazakhstan this week to process Russian crude outside the country, which would see 70% of the refined fuel shipped back to Russia. Oil will need to be delivered to the refinery by rail as the facility is not connected to a Russian pipeline, according to reports. This summer has also seen big increases in the amount of fuel Russia imports from its Ukraine war ally Belarus. Imports this June increased by a staggering factor of 141 compared with June last year. Kremlin officials had expressed hope earlier in the summer that Russia might be turning a corner in its fuel crisis, but instead August has seen a new intensification. At least six Russian regions have reinstated or tightened restrictions on gasoline sales and a new wave of Ukrainian strikes on oil processing facilities completely shut down the Orsk refinery . Russia’s deputy prime minister, Alexander Novak, who in ​July had said Russia would begin importing oil products to help stabilise the domestic market, this week described the country’s energy situation as “constantly changing” as he said some refineries were back in operation. “The situation is changing every day. We’re constantly monitoring it and are making decisions at our headquarters. We’re gathering the federal headquarters with the regions and all of our companies twice a week,” he said. The aim of Kyiv’s campaign is to bring the cost of the war in Ukraine back to Moscow. In the midst of an international sanctions regime that has already damaged Russia’s economy, the Ukrainian strikes on refineries – which have intensified in the last two months – are not only hitting a source of revenue that has been used to pay for Vladimir Putin’s war, but have prompted serious domestic shortages that even the latest efforts appear unable to mitigate. Ukraine has so far in August carried out 18 attacks on Russian refineries, matching the previous month’s record. Even before Ukraine stepped up its campaign against refineries, output had dropped by 28%, according to industry analysts. Writing in June , retired Australian general Mick Ryan predicted Ukraine would only increase its efforts to hit Russian oil production. “Putin has never retreated, in public, from his maximalist ambition to subjugate Ukraine. The strikes are not designed to change his rhetoric; they are designed to change his calculus,” he wrote. “Strategy, in the end, is a contest of competing calculations, and Ukraine’s bet is that sustained pressure on Russia’s economic foundations will, over time, force a recalculation that battlefield performance could not. This will not happen quickly, and it may not happen at all. But it denies Putin his longstanding assumption that time is on his side.” That was echoed last month in a commentary for the Royal United Services Institute by Petras Katinas and Natia Seskuria. “Russia’s fuel shortages are becoming a budget problem. Ukraine’s sustained strikes on Russian refineries are not only damaging infrastructure and squeezing Russia’s oil industry, they are forcing the Kremlin to spend more to keep fuel flowing at home while earning less from exports. That trade-off is becoming increasingly expensive.” And the biggest damage being inflicted is also likely the hardest to detect, they added. “Export restrictions prevent refiners from selling into higher-priced foreign markets, reducing foreign currency earnings while limiting companies’ ability to recover costs at home.”

title: Geelong fined $140,000 over secret Jake Kolodjashnij concussion waiver
text: Geelong fined $140,000 over secret Jake Kolodjashnij concussion waiver. A schism has emerged at the top of the AFL over whether clubs can avoid future liability for head injuries, despite the league fining Geelong $140,000 for failing to lodge the concussion waiver signed by defender Jake Kolodjashnij. The Cats sanction was made of two parts, including $100,000 for failing to inform the AFL of a change to Kolodjashnij’s contract, previously described as a “waiver” by AFL Commission chair and former Cats president Craig Drummond. Related: From the Pocket: Geelong is a club that pushes its luck but the concussion story must not be buried That also activated a $40,000 suspended fine applied to Geelong for salary cap-related breaches last year, leaving the club with a $140,000 penalty to be paid into the AFL’s injury and support fund. The Cats recorded a profit of $1.7m last year. Geelong accepted the findings of the independent review and acknowledged the sanction in a statement on Thursday. AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon was unequivocal when saying a concussion waiver like Kolodjashnij’s would not be approved, were it to be lodged with the AFL and AFL Players’ Association (AFLPA) as required. “It can’t happen and it won’t happen,” he said. “What would have happened is there would have been a line of inquiry and the AFLPA would have been involved.” Barely an hour later Drummond was more ambiguous, initially saying he was not aware of Dillon’s comment, and then adding that the question over whether such a waiver would be approved was “hypothetical”. When asked to explain the discrepancy between his view and Dillon’s, Drummond said there will be a “significant set of discussions” between the AFLPA, the AFL and clubs over the “protocols and the process for these types of situations”. “I certainly, as chair of the AFL, I don’t want any of our clubs or any of our players being put in this situation,” he said. “We need some clarity around where there’s been a bit more grey, we need a bit more clarity.” Drummond appeared to be referring to a review of the safety nets around concussion that the AFL and AFLPA also announced today, covering issues like the challenges of commercial insurance protection for players and officials, and an increase to the scope of the injury and support fund. Dillon said earlier the AFL had work to do to better manage risk to players, board members, clubs and doctors. “The challenge that’s facing the industry as a whole is how risk is looked at, how the insurance is looked at, and how the safety net for the players and officials is looked at, so, that’s where we’re at now.” The clause in Kolodjashnij’s contract was drafted and signed after the defender was not fully cleared by the AFL’s concussion panel in 2024, and followed consultation about potential risks of returning to senior football with the player, his family, doctors and insurers. The waiver was set aside by Geelong in the days after its existence first became public. The AFL Commission found the Cats did not intend to conceal the agreement, however, in accepting the recommendations from an investigation by Kings Counsel James Peters. Commission member Paul Bassat said despite the sanction for the “unauthorised variation”, Geelong had acted with the health and safety of its players in mind. “It is clear this incident goes beyond the breach of lodgement rules, and has raised broader issues to do with informed consent in playing contact sport and the paramount responsibilities for players’ health and safety.” The sanction exceeds recent fines issued by the AFL, including the $77,500 penalty to the Cats for salary cap breaches, of which $40,000 was suspended, and the $75,000 fine handed to Carlton for their mismanagement of Elijah Hollands’ mental health episode . The amount, however, is minimal compared to the compensation likely to be sought by past players as they pursue the football industry in a head injury-related class action, with former Cat Max Rooke as lead plaintiff, which includes more than 100 former AFL players and is expected to go to trial next year. There has been widespread criticism directed at Geelong for developing the waiver which has also enveloped the AFL given Drummond, the former Cats president, became chair of the AFL Commission in March. Drummond has already apologised for “the mistakes made in this very complex situation” , but said on Thursday it was “administrative failure” in failing to lodge the document. “It’s not the board’s role to lodge documents or arrange where the documents end up going,” he said. “Management clearly made a decision not to lodge the document, but it was clearly a conscious decision because they didn’t feel that they needed to lodge the documents,” he said. “The mistake made was the documentation was not lodged, and with that lodgment there may have come up conversations, presumably with either the PA (AFLPA) or the AFL.” Drummond recused himself from the AFL’s deliberation on the matter.

title: ‘If you harm my project, I’ll harm you’: former NSW official tells Icac about fugitive developer’s call
text: ‘If you harm my project, I’ll harm you’: former NSW official tells Icac about fugitive developer’s call. A fugitive Sydney developer allegedly warned the then-New South Wales building commissioner that he would “harm” him if he got in the way of his projects which were being inspected for defects, the corruption watchdog has heard. Giving evidence to the Independent Commission against Corruption on Thursday, David Chandler described an interaction he had with Toplace developments’ Jean Nassif. “He just basically said: Don’t you harm my project, and if you harm my project, I’ll harm you,” Chandler said, recalling a phone call with Nassif in 2021. Related: Cults, setups and rumours: years after their downfalls, former NSW Liberal MPs are exacting revenge The pair had already clashed in person in 2020 at a meeting where Chandler said Nassif had become “loud and overbearing”. Chandler had ordered a “destructive inspection” of a Toplace building in Botany, meaning bathrooms would need to be ripped up to check the waterproofing. Chandler said on Thursday that after the 2021 phone call, he banned Nassif from being present on sites when he was conducting inspections, and resolved not to deal with him directly. A few days before the phone call in April 2021, Chandler put a prohibition order on Skyview, a Toplace apartment complex in Castle Hill, preventing it from being occupied. Icac is investigating whether payments to a group of young conservatives known as the Reformers amounted to illegal political donations to the NSW Liberal party. It is investigating whether $2m allegedly paid by Nassif to Jeremy Greenwood, Christian Ellis and Charles Perrottet, the brother of the former premier Dominic Perrottet, were made to achieve certain outcomes, including the removal of the building commissioner. Chandler is not under investigation by Icac. Nassif, who fled Australia for rural Lebanon in 2022, is expected to appear before the commission by video link from Lebanon next week. He has previously denied any wrongdoing. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email In April 2021, the Greens senator David Shoebridge and others sent Chandler photos of substantial cracking in the Skyview building’s basement prompting urgent action, Chandler said. Chandler said over the five years he was commissioner he undertook hundreds of inspections, but he was aware Nassif believed he was being singled out. Soon after the phone call, Chandler became aware of “an accumulation of pressure”, the former commissioner told Icac. He became aware politicians had been told by figures in the industry he was “on the take” and journalists were being offered material that sought to undermine his integrity. “It seemed to be an intentional campaign to white ant me,” Chandler told Icac. The first example of the alleged pressure campaign was an anonymous email to Toplace suggesting that if $5m was paid to a lawyer, William Roberts, the building commissioner would lift orders that were holding up occupancy certificates for Toplace’s developments. The email was raised with Chandler by executives at Toplace, including Sharangan Maheswaran, who is a person of interest at the Icac inquiry. The Toplace executives described it as an “attempt at a shakedown”, Chandler said. Chandler suggested he and the Toplace executives immediately go to the police, but Maheswaran said they were not sure about its origins and were still investigating. Chandler took contemporaneous notes and reported it to his departmental head, Emma Hogan, who ordered an internal audit. Icac heard Toplace executives did not engage with the departmental inquiry, and Chandler was cleared. “So they could see that this – that is the extortion attempt allegation – was going to be of no assistance in getting the occupation certificate?” the counsel assisting, Juliet Curtin, asked. “None,” Chandler replied. The second example of an alleged pressure campaign was a video which showed Chandler telling workers on a building site that he had an “informal list” of dodgy certifiers which he had provided to the banks. In the video Chandler says the industry needs to become more professional. The inquiry heard the video was reported by The Australian in June 2022, with the paper suggesting it showed Chandler had misled an earlier parliamentary committee about whether he regulated certifiers. It led to another internal investigation by Hogan and the department. Chandler was cleared, but it was suggested he undertake internal training. The video was also raised with the then-minister for fair trading, Eleni Petinos, who was Chandler’s boss at the time. Related: ‘You have got to go’: former NSW minister tells Icac ‘something strange at play’ when she was sacked by Perrottet Petinos and her chief of staff, Cassandra Lawry, gave evidence last week about being shown the video by Chris Spence, the chief of staff to the then-planning minister, Anthony Roberts, in May 2022 and it having been raised on other occasions in June of that year. Petinos and Lawry both told the commission they later came to believe that they were being used in a campaign to destabilise the commissioner. Petinos, Lawry and Spence are not persons of interest in the inquiry. Petinos had replaced the former minister, Kevin Anderson, in a reshuffle when Dominic Perrottet became premier in October 2021. In a tape played during the opening of the inquiry, Nassif was heard to say that Perrottet had agreed to replace the fair trading minister, Kevin Anderson, with Petinos, whom he described as “my girl”. Chandler said he had noticed at the time a couple of media stories that appeared to discredit the minister. “So there was just that atmosphere of, he’s not doing a good job or that his role is under review,” he said. In July 2022 Chandler resigned, citing a lack of confidence in him from the minister and undue pressure from developers. “I just didn’t want to risk being asked to leave a role with a shadow like that. So I thought, well, the best thing to do is to avoid that risk,” he said. “So whether I was overreaching in how I felt at the time, I can’t speculate on that now, but I would have been very, very unhappy with having the final day in office being that I had lost the confidence of the minister and that the secretary was asked to make other arrangements.” Chandler was later reinstated and served as building commissioner until 2024. The inquiry continues.
